content.thinking:
Checking the io-shop HighErrorRate incident: the monthly-spend flag was switched on at 18:15:47, and ZeroDivisionErrors started right after. Argus reverted it at 18:22:13, but the logs show the flag still evaluating as on through 18:25 and errors continuing, so that mitigation didn't hold and the flag went back on at T22.

I'm ruling out a deploy as the cause: the deploys I read back show nothing in the window before onset, and the replicas all run one revision with no partial rollout. The flag change at 18:15:47 looks like the only change before the errors started.

I'm ruling out a deploy in the 18 hours before the onset, since the record shows no deploy in that window. The log lines from 17:45 to 18:14 also show the service healthy with the flag off, so the running revision alone doesn't look harmful. I'll cite the earlier health metrics for that as well.

Next I'm tracing the chain step by step: the errors come from the account-page path at spend_summary.py:47, and that path is reached because the monthly-spend flag was switched on at 18:15:47. The last step is that the monthly average divides by this month's purchases, which would be zero for shoppers who haven't bought anything yet.

Working out the root cause now: the monthly path that the flag turns on divides by this month's purchase count with no zero guard, so shoppers with past purchases but none this month hit a ZeroDivisionError at the spend_summary line and their account page fails.

Now I'm spelling out the root cause in plain terms: turning on the new feature routes account pages through a monthly spending calculation that likely fails for shoppers who haven't bought anything this month. The flag is back on, so those failures could continue for them until the fix ships or the flag is actually off.

I'm checking whether the fix can actually stop the failures, since the flag is back on and the earlier revert never reached the service. Switching it off at the provider apparently didn't take effect, so I'd need the service's own evaluations to show it off, and the ZeroDivisionError lines to stop and the error rate to return to baseline.

I'm sketching the stop-the-harm step now: switching monthly-spend-feature off again and making sure io-shop's replicas actually pick that up, then checking the service's own logs for the flag evaluating off, the ZeroDivisionError lines stopping, and the error rate returning to baseline. Next I want to find out why the earlier switch-off at the flag provider never reached the service, whether caching, polling, or something else is holding the replicas on.

Now I'm listing contributing factors: first, no test seems to have covered the monthly path for shoppers with no purchases this month before the flag went on, and I'm proposing a review step for flagged code paths. Second, the flag reached all traffic at once, with about a quarter of requests on at 18:15.

Next I'm weighing whether the monthly-spend flag coming on for all requests within a minute counts as an all-at-once rollout, since I saw no staged rollout in the logs. I'll propose gradual rollouts with an automatic halt on error rate. I'm also noting that nobody was paged, and wondering whether that alert-to-paging gap was itself a contributing factor.

I'm now looking at the contributing factors that held before the incident. The alert fired on io-shop but paged nobody, which could have let a person intervene sooner. The flag-off change never reached what the service was evaluating, so the earlier revert couldn't have ended the errors, and that propagation gap is worth recording on its own.

I'm weighing whether the alert needs a detection rule that flags when the service's evaluated flag state disagrees with the flag provider, since that mismatch is what the logs showed after the revert. I'm also noting an earlier incident that tried reverting this same flag and was refuted, and I want to check whether that history is relevant to the contributing factors.

Next I'm considering whether an earlier incident that tried reverting this same flag, and got refuted, points to a contributing factor: the fault may have been left in place after that one, and I haven't seen any follow-up that would have stopped the flag from being switched on again.

I'm weighing whether the revert that didn't take effect should count as a factor in its own right, but the flag-propagation gap is already covered as a contributing factor, so I'll leave it out of the list of what went wrong during the response.

I'm checking the "went wrong" side now: C2 was marked refuted on the strength of C1's test, even though C2 itself noted the revert never reached the service, so it was never tested on its own. That's a gap worth recording. Nobody was paged, which I'll keep as a finding under the contributing factors.

Now I'm looking at what went well during the response: the investigator placed the start at 18:15, matching the flag switch, and the revert and the later re-enable were both timed. The investigator also caught the flag still evaluating as on after the revert, and the code-fix agent proposed a draft PR.

Now I'm drafting the action items: one to gate flagged code paths behind tests that cover accounts with no purchases this month, one to roll flag changes out in stages with an automatic halt on error rate, one to route the io-shop HighErrorRate alert to on-call paging, and one to alert when io-shop's logged flag evaluations disagree with the provider's state after a change.

Now I'm checking whether the revision running on all replicas, which the history doesn't name, was healthy with the flag off before 18:14.

I'm now checking the mechanism behind the incident: an admin switched monthly-spend-feature on, and from that moment the evaluations for account page requests moved to on. Those requests then raised ZeroDivisionError in the spend summary code, and the failures held from the onset minute through the last minute I read. I'm also considering why the system let a flag go on over a path that hadn't been tested, which points back to the contributing factors I already listed.

Now I'm noting that the symptom needs a plain description, so I'll call it account pages failing for shoppers and tie the timing to the flag-switch moment, then I'll check the lessons-learned items so each one starts with who timed it.

action_items.item: Before a feature flag can be switched on in production, require tests that exercise the code path it enables, including edge cases such as a shopper with no purchases this month.
Roll out io-shop feature flags to a small share of requests first, and stop the rollout automatically when the error rate rises.
Link the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop to on-call paging so that a person is paged when it fires.
Alert when the flag state io-shop logs that it evaluates disagrees with the flag provider's state after a flag change.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' account page requests failed with server errors, starting in the onset minute and continuing through the last minute read.
The failing account page requests raised ZeroDivisionError in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py. These errors appear in io-shop's logs from the onset minute onwards and not before it.

ruled_out.what: A deploy: none came back over the window read before the onset.

The revision running on every replica, which the history does not name. With it in place and the flag off, account pages rendered normally and the flag evaluated off in every minute read before the onset.

causal_chain.step: An admin switched the feature flag monthly-spend-feature on at {P1.1}. In that same minute, flag evaluations started moving from off to on, and from the next minute every evaluation came back on, which sent account page requests down the flag's monthly path.
The monthly path likely divides by the number of purchases made this month, which is zero for shoppers who have bought nothing this month.

input.cause_in_plain_words: An admin switched on a new feature that sent shoppers' account pages through a monthly spending calculation, and that calculation likely fails for anyone who has bought nothing so far this month.

contributing_factors.factor: No check was seen that exercised the monthly path behind monthly-spend-feature for a shopper with no purchases this month before the flag was switched on in production. By Code-Fix's reading, the tests in the file it read did not cover that case.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The division by zero would have been found before the flag was switched on, and account pages would not have failed.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: No staged rollout of the flag was seen. From the minute after it was switched on, every evaluation of monthly-spend-feature in io-shop came back on.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Only a small share of account page requests would have taken the failing path at first, and a halt on rising errors could have stopped it before it reached everyone.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: The HighErrorRate alert on io-shop paged nobody: no on-call incident was linked to it.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A person would have known about the failures as soon as the alert fired and could have stepped in when the automated revert did not take effect, shortening the incident.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

contributing_factors.factor: Switching monthly-spend-feature off in the flag provider did not change what io-shop evaluated: its logs kept showing the flag on after it was switched off.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Switching the flag off would have taken account pages off the failing path and ended the failures without waiting for a code fix.
contributing_factors.label: CF-4

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent dated the start of the incident to the minute the flag was switched on.
The Investigator Agent linked the failures to monthly-spend-feature being switched on and to the ZeroDivisionError in the account page logs.
The Mitigation Agent switched monthly-spend-feature off, a step that can be undone.
The Mitigation Agent put the flag back on once switching it off did not help, leaving the service as it found it.
The Investigator Agent noticed that io-shop's logs still showed the flag evaluating on after it was switched off.
The Code-Fix Agent opened a draft pull request with a proposed fix for a person to review.

went_wrong: C2 was marked refuted because of the test run for C1, even though C2 itself said that switching the flag off had not reached the service. The one action taken never got account pages off the monthly path, so it could not show whether the flag was the cause, and Argus moved on with no explanation left to try.

input.root_cause: The monthly path that monthly-spend-feature switches on works out a shopper's average spend per item this month by dividing the month's total by the number of purchases made this month. Nothing guards against that number being zero, so for every shopper who has bought before but not this month, line {F1.1} of src/io_shop/spend_summary.py raises ZeroDivisionError and the account page request fails.
input.still_at_risk: With monthly-spend-feature back on, account pages could keep failing for every shopper who has bought nothing this month, and switching the flag off in the flag provider might again not change what io-shop evaluates.
input.stops_the_harm: Switch monthly-spend-feature off again in a way that reaches every io-shop replica. Confirm at the service that io-shop's logs show the flag evaluating off, that the ZeroDivisionError lines from src/io_shop/spend_summary.py stop, and that the error rate falls back to about {errors_before}.
input.why_it_did_not_help: Find out why io-shop kept evaluating monthly-spend-feature as on after it was switched off in the flag provider at {P2.1}: whether the change reached the replicas at all, or was held back by caching, polling or another source of flag values. If it did reach them, find out why account pages kept failing.
